title: Browser Agents and Long-Horizon Web Tasks

questions.question: A browser agent reads a page written by an unknown site and then submits a form. What makes this workflow especially risky?
options: The agent cannot access authenticated sessions
A form submission is always a read-only action
Browser pages contain no instructions that models can read
Untrusted content can influence a consequential write
questions.explanation: A browser agent reads untrusted page content but can submit forms using the user’s authority, so page text can influence a consequential write. Authenticated access is part of the risk, not something browser agents lack.

questions.question: A fetched page contains the phrase ignore previous instructions and requests an exfiltration post. Which defense in the demo strips this visible-text pattern?
options: The URL fragment parser
The permission-mode budget cap
The content sanitizer
The benchmark task verifier
questions.explanation: The sanitizer scans visible HTML for known phrases and strips matches; it does not parse URL fragments. A fragment parser would be a different component, not the defense that catches this visible-text pattern.

questions.question: A malicious command is hidden in a URL fragment, which the sanitizer does not inspect. What defense can still block the resulting write?
options: A retry that submits the write a second time
A longer agent context that preserves the page details
A read/write boundary that rejects page-originated writes
A benchmark score that counts the URL as a task
questions.explanation: The read/write boundary checks the origin of a consequential action and blocks a write initiated by page content even when the URL fragment escaped sanitization. Retrying the same write would repeat the risk.

questions.question: Which benchmark is intended to measure an agent operating a full desktop with mouse, keyboard, and shell?
options: SWE-bench Pro
OSWorld
BrowseComp
WebArena-Verified
questions.explanation: OSWorld measures full desktop operation with mouse, keyboard, and shell. BrowseComp tests web fact-finding, while WebArena-Verified measures transactional web workflows.

questions.question: A browser agent follows a URL-fragment instruction to post a session token. The sanitizer only sees HTML, while the write boundary rejects page-originated actions. What result should occur?
options: Both defenses approve because the fragment is not visible
The sanitizer can miss it, but the write boundary blocks the post
The write boundary blocks every read before the page loads
The sanitizer removes the fragment and approves the post
questions.explanation: The URL fragment enters model context even though the HTML sanitizer misses it; the page-originated post is then blocked by the read/write boundary. The two controls cover different parts of the attack path.

questions.question: A task requires browsing authenticated pages and making external changes. Which deployment control set best follows the lesson?
options: One broad permission grant reused across every browser task
Scoped credentials, write approval, request logs, and session isolation
HTML sanitization alone with no distinction between reads and writes
Production credentials, unrestricted egress, and no action records
questions.explanation: Scoped credentials, session isolation, retained request logs, and approval for consequential writes limit exposure across the workflow. Sanitization alone cannot stop every injection or multi-step exfiltration path.
